stories.title: War and heat: Why are wheat prices soaring?
stories.summary: Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on their respective grain terminals in the Black Sea as drought impact wheat production. Wheat prices have risen sharply amid disruptions to Black Sea exports as the Russia-Ukraine war continues and as changing weather patterns cause droughts that have sharply reduced production. Over the past month, Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on each other’s grain terminals on the Black Sea. With Russia the world’s largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine among the top 10 grain-producing countries, these attacks have taken their toll on global wheat and grain supply. Chicago wheat futures, the global benchmark for the grain market, hit a three-year high on Friday, before nudging down 0.54 percent on Monday to $7.79 per bushel by 02:00 GMT. Authorities in Russia’s Rostov region called a state of emergency on Friday after announcing that port closures and navigation disruptions in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea basin have led to a pile-up of agricultural products at farms. Meanwhile, the rising temperatures and lack of rain have threatened to cut this year’s wheat harvest in South Africa’s Swartland, which produces about 20 percent of the country’s wheat. What impact is the Russia-Ukraine war having on prices? Over the past month, strikes on ports, vessels and grain facilities amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict have disrupted grain terminals and forced shippers to delay or cancel cargo loadings during the peak export season. While Russian missile attacks have impacted Ukraine’s grain exports, Ukraine’s drone attacks in the Sea of Azov have also sharply curtailed Russian shipments of both grain and wheat. At the same time, attacks on Russia’s Novorossiysk and Taman ports have increased shipping costs out of its Black Sea ports. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Infrastructure, in July, Ukraine suffered 35 Russian attacks on vessels in port, 22 at sea and 67 on port facilities.

stories.title: 'She slipped out of my hand' - couple's children missing after ferry capsizes
stories.summary: Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people. Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus. She and her husband, Hayri, survived and, like many other families, are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search. "She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears. Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands. "It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled. The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island.

stories.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
stories.summary: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks Airlink insist flyby conducted according to regulations A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town. Continue reading...
stories.headline: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash

opening: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks Airlink insist flyby conducted according to regulations.

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.
body: The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.
Footage of the flyover quickly began circulating on social media, prompting mixed reactions as some expressed concerns over safety.
A South African airline has defended a low-level flying stunt over a packed-out rugby stadium in Cape Town on the weekend.
Two Airlink-operated jets soared just above city's DHL Stadium ahead of a test match between South Africa and New Zealand, prompting cheers from the reported crowd of more than 50,000 below.
According to flight-tracking firm Flightradar24, the lead aircraft flew roughly just 41 to 46 feet above the roof of the stadium.
In a statement on Sunday, Airlink defended the manoeuvre.
“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” the carrier said.
“The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude at around 150 knots.
The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby,” it added.
The airline also shared footage and images of the move in a post on X, writing: "Planning.
Precision.
Performance."

stories.title: France's politicians look to close gap with far right ahead of key election
stories.summary: With eight months until the next french Presidential election, politicians are ramping up their campaigning, with interviews, meetings and public statements. But who exactly will run has yet to be decided. The centre-left socialists and Place Publique parties will hold a primary in October to elect one candidate, as to not dilute the vote. While centrist and centre-right candidates are also having to decide between rivalry and unity. The dilemma? How to best stave off the rise of the far right and left.

stories.title: FIFA enlists PR firm to rehabilitate Gianni Infantino’s image — UK daily
stories.summary: According to The Times, the agreement was signed in March 2025 and it runs through the end of 2026
article_sentences: LONDON, August 31.
The world’s governing body of football, FIFA, has allegedly signed a contract with the London-based marketing agency.
Ten Toes Media for an approximate sum of $3.1 million to improve the image of the organization and its President Gianni Infantino, The Times reported on Monday.
According to the British-based daily, the agreement was signed in March 2025 and it runs through the end of 2026.
A copy of the contract that the daily provided states that the agency was responsible for overseeing FIFA's social media accounts.

Infantino announced a proposal on July 30 to sell a share of the FIFA World Cup commercial rights to private investors under a scheme that he claimed would have potentially brought in tens of millions of dollars.
The plan involved establishing a company that would control the major men's and women's FIFA tournaments - the FIFA World Cup and the FIFA Club World Cup.
The organization consulted with people close to the administration of US President Donald Trump prior to voicing this decision.
In March 2023, Infantino was re-elected for another four-year term as the president of FIFA.
Infantino, who was 52 at that time, ran unopposed as he was elected unanimously at the 2023 FIFA Congress in the Rwandan capital of Kigali.
Infantino was elected the president of the world’s governing body in February 2016 at the FIFA Extraordinary Congress in Paris.
In June 2019, he was re-elected for another four-year presidential term.

stories.title: Climate crisis pushes French winemakers to bet on warmer future in Brittany and Normandy
stories.summary: As rising temperatures reshape France's vineyards, winemakers are turning to Normandy and Brittany, regions once known for cider, not grapes. Those fleeing harsher conditions in traditional areas like the Loire Valley see opportunity up north, though some warn the same climate volatility disrupting southern vineyards is starting to follow them there.
